note: Re-recorded once for four changes that landed together: run-an-entry-without-root, retire-an-entry-a-build-no-longer-names, probe-a-service-before-it-counts-as-live and unseal-a-value-after-a-reboot. Each adds a declared fact the planner reads, and one recording for the set is deliberate: recording per change would have re-recorded the same counters four times. Sixty-seven of the eighty-one gated figures rose and fourteen fell, none by more than 5.2% per entry, which is what says this is the incremental cost of four fields rather than a regression. Five readings account for it: a machine's scope and its seal recipient are read once per machine, a unit's probe and its bound are read for every unit of every entry and the probe count is folded once per entry, the machine record carries the recipient as an explicit absence, the delivery set is walked a second time for the machines that state no recipient, and the per-machine unsealer reading asks varsPathsDeep of every placed entry's units and configData. nrOpUpdateValuesCopied is the counter that moved most in relative terms (+5.1% on the largest fixtures) and it is also the one with no slack at all: a new top-level key on the right of the `korora // { ... }` in lib/atoms.nix costs exactly one copied value per plan, measured, which is why the probe change's isZeroDuration rides atoms.domains and the privileged-port boundary rides portRange. list.elements fell between 3.7% and 4.6% across every fleet and mesh size, so the growth bound improved while the constant cost rose.

growth.note: The bound applies to every fixture measured at more than one size, and it is 1.25 because the cost per plan entry has to stay flat as the fleet grows: `fleet` grows the number of entries and keeps each entry's own work constant, `mesh` grows one entry's work with the fleet and keeps the plan linear in it, and a quarter of slack absorbs constant-factor noise without admitting any super-linear term.
